item.title: Interpreting a Correlation Between Temperature and Bike Rentals
item.stimulus: A bike-share company recorded, for each of 60 randomly selected days, the daily high temperature in degrees Fahrenheit and the number of bikes rented that day. Technology reports a correlation coefficient of r = 0.91 for these data.

parts.prompt: Interpret the value of r in context.

criteria.text: Interprets the sign of r = 0.91 as a positive association: as daily high temperature increases, number of bikes rented tends to increase.
criteria.evidence: Response links the positive sign of r to the direction of the association in context.
criteria.fix: Read the sign of r as direction, then restate it in context using both variable names.

criteria.text: States that r = 0.91, which is close to 1, indicates a strong linear association between daily high temperature and number of bikes rented.
criteria.evidence: Response says the linear association is strong because r is close to 1, naming the two variables.
criteria.fix: Say how close r is to -1 or 1, call the linear association strong, moderate or weak, and name both variables.

parts.prompt: A manager says, "Because r = 0.91, a linear model is definitely appropriate for predicting number of bikes rented from daily high temperature." Explain why this reasoning is incomplete and what should be done before deciding that a linear model is appropriate.

criteria.text: States that a value of r as close to -1 or 1 as 0.91 does not by itself show that a linear model is appropriate.
criteria.evidence: Response says a correlation coefficient near -1 or 1 does not necessarily mean a linear model is appropriate.
criteria.fix: Remember r only measures linear association strength; a strong r can still come from a curved pattern, so r alone cannot justify a linear model.

criteria.text: States that a residual plot (or scatterplot) should be examined for curvature or other pattern before concluding a linear model is appropriate.
criteria.evidence: Response names a residual plot or a scatterplot as the check and says a pattern such as curvature would show the linear model is not appropriate.
criteria.fix: Name the check: make a residual plot and look for curvature; a random scatter supports a linear model.

parts.prompt: A manager also concludes that warmer temperatures cause more bikes to be rented. Is this conclusion justified by the correlation? Explain.

criteria.text: States that correlation does not imply causation, so the association does not show that warmer temperatures cause more bikes to be rented.
criteria.evidence: Response says an association or correlation, even a strong one, does not show that one variable causes changes in the other.
criteria.fix: Whenever a claim says one variable causes another, point out that a strong association does not establish causation.

parts.prompt: The analysts will also measure daily high temperature in different units, in degrees Celsius instead of degrees Fahrenheit. What value of r will they find for the new measurements? Explain.

criteria.text: States that r would still be 0.91 after measuring temperature in degrees Celsius instead of degrees Fahrenheit because r is unit-free.
criteria.evidence: Response says r is unchanged and gives unit-free (not affected by the units of measurement) as the reason.
criteria.fix: Recall that r has no units, so changing the units of either variable by a positive-slope conversion leaves r unchanged.

item.model_answer:
(a) The correlation r = 0.91 is positive, so as daily high temperature increases, number of bikes rented tends to increase. Because r is close to 1, the linear association between daily high temperature and number of bikes rented is strong.

(b) A value of r close to -1 or 1 does not necessarily mean a linear model is appropriate. The data could follow a curved pattern even when r is large. The analysts should look at a residual plot (or a scatterplot) and check for curvature or another pattern before deciding.

(c) No. Correlation does not imply causation. The strong association does not show that warmer temperatures cause more bikes to be rented; other variables could account for the pattern.

(d) The new r will still be 0.91. The correlation coefficient is unit-free, so changing the units of measurement (measuring temperature in degrees Celsius instead of degrees Fahrenheit) does not change r.
item.verification_python:
import math
def reg(x, y):
    n = len(x); mx = sum(x) / n; my = sum(y) / n
    sxx = sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x); syy = sum((b - my) ** 2 for b in y)
    sxy = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y)); b = sxy / sxx
    return b, my - b * mx, sxy / math.sqrt(sxx * syy), mx, my
r = 0.91
assert -1 <= r <= 1 and abs(r) > 0.8
assert (r < 0) == False
xs = [40, 52, 61, 70, 78, 85, 91]
ys = [210, 305, 330, 420, 515, 560, 640]
r1 = reg(xs, ys)[2]
r2 = reg([5/9 * x for x in xs], ys)[2]
assert abs(r1 - r2) < 1e-12
print("ALL_CHECKS_PASSED")

failed: rubric_points: Part (a), criterion a2 requires an explicit explanation that r is close to 1, although the part asks only for an interpretation. A complete interpretation stating a strong, positive linear association in context should earn both points without that additional justification.

solution: The independent solution agrees with the rubric's substantive conclusions: strong positive linear association, correlation alone insufficient to establish model appropriateness or causation, and unchanged r = 0.91 under Celsius conversion. However, its complete interpretation in part (a) could lose a2 solely because it does not explicitly say that 0.91 is close to 1; that additional justification should not be required.
